item.title: 【回复】@StockSavvyShay：内幕人士买入为ASTS带来良好市场情绪提振
item.description:
被回答的问题 @VanquishTrader
$ASTS COULD BE THE BIGGEST STEAL OF 2026

I think one of the more interesting developments surrounding AST is that board member Adriana Cisneros just purchased another $1M worth of shares on the open market at an average price of $23.54, following approximately $620K in purchases back in August when the stock was trading around $57.

What makes the timing particularly interesting is that AST SpaceMobile has now fallen more than 80% from its all-time high near $133, while the market appears to be increasingly confusing the company's execution challenges with a deterioration in its long-term opportunity.

The distinction matters because AST's technology, carrier relationships and broader commercial opportunity are considerably more developed than they were when shares traded at significantly higher levels.

I would never interpret insider buying as confirmation that a stock has bottomed, but seeing a board member commit additional capital after such an enormous drawdown certainly makes me question whether the market has become too pessimistic about what this business could eventually become.

And I think the biggest distinction investors need to understand is that proving satellite connectivity works and building a commercially viable telecommunications network are two very different things.

AST has already demonstrated that its satellites can connect ordinary smartphones and successfully hand off connections between terrestrial and satellite networks but providing reliable, continuous coverage across its priority markets requires approximately 45 to 60 BlueBirds in orbit which is where the launch delays pushing meaningful service expansion into 2027 become particularly important.

What gives me confidence is that manufacturing is progressing toward six satellites per month, while the introduction of next-generation ASICs could substantially increase the processing capacity of future BlueBirds.

But ultimately, manufacturing additional satellites only creates economic value once those satellites reach orbit, become operational and begin supporting paying customers which is why I think investors should be focusing less on the number of satellites being produced and more on how much usable network capacity and recurring revenue each additional deployment can generate.

What makes the opportunity particularly compelling is that AST is not simply building a satellite network to provide coverage in remote areas, but potentially establishing an entirely new layer of global communications infrastructure that can serve commercial telecommunications, government applications and sovereign connectivity requirements using much of the same underlying technology.

That distinction could become increasingly important as its existing carrier relationships provide access to established customer networks without requiring AST to independently build an enormous consumer distribution business, while its expanding government and international partnerships create additional opportunities to monetize the constellation.

I think the market is still underestimating how much larger that opportunity could eventually become, particularly if AST can demonstrate that the same satellite infrastructure supports multiple revenue streams as network capacity expands.

Of course, none of those opportunities should be confused with revenue already being generated, but I believe the company is building toward something considerably more valuable than the relatively narrow satellite connectivity business investors initially associated with it.

Now, I completely understand why the market remains skeptical because AST still faces substantial launch, financing and competitive risks, and the company needs to demonstrate that its expanding constellation can generate enough recurring revenue to justify the enormous capital required to build it.

What I want to see over the next several quarters is the existing launch backlog converting into operational satellites, initial commercial service expanding into meaningful customer adoption and improving economics as greater network utilization allows each additional satellite to generate more revenue.

If those milestones materialize without excessive dilution, I think investors could eventually look back at current prices as one of the more extraordinary opportunities of this AI and space infrastructure cycle.

And that's ultimately why I find Adriana Cisneros's latest purchase so interesting, because while buying another $1M in shares doesn't guarantee the stock has bottomed, it raises a much bigger question about whether the market has become so focused on AST's near-term execution problems that it's overlooking the long-term value of the global communications infrastructure the company is building.

item.title: 【回复】@ArtificialAnlys：测试显示Octen Search快速动态模式每项任务消耗约11.9万个Token
item.description:
回复 @ArtificialAnlys
Octen Search (fast, dynamic) returns each search in ~0.17s, the fastest of the 25 Search API products we benchmark, and scores 82 on the Artificial Analysis Search Index

We benchmarked the fast, dynamic mode of @OctenAI's Search API in our Stirrup agent harness with Octen Search as its web_search tool to complete 1700 search-focused tasks.

In our September run, Octen Search (highlights) scored 77. In these November runs, Octen Search (fast, dynamic) scores 82.

Key benchmarking results for Octen Search:

➤ Speed: each search returns in about 0.17s, the lowest of the 25 Search API products and about half the next lowest (0.33s). Time per Task is 13.3s, the lowest of 26 and comparable to Parallel Search (fast, objective) (14.3s) and Keenable Search (realtime) (14.4s), against a board median of about 26s

➤ Artificial Analysis Search Index: 82, 3rd of 26, within 1 point of Parallel Search (advanced, objective) and Keenable Search (pro) at 83. That is a ~49-point lift over the same model with no search (33). No product scores higher in less time

➤ BrowseComp: Octen scores 92% on our hard BrowseComp subset (200 questions), the highest of 26 and ~4 points above Keenable Search (pro) and Perplexity Search (medium) at 87%. Octen scores 84 F1 on DeepSearchQA (7th) and 72% on AA-Omniscience (joint 6th)

➤ Low cost: about $0.018 per task, 3rd lowest of 26 behind TinyFish ($0.009) and Parallel Search (fast, objective) ($0.014), against a board median of $0.063

Key details:

➤ Setup: GPT-5.6 Luna (medium) in Stirrup, Octen Search API with result_type=dynamic

➤ Dynamic results: Octen returns only the results it finds relevant, up to the 10 we request, and sets the highlight length for each result

➤ Pricing: $1 per 1k requests
原帖

回复 @ArtificialAnlys
Time per Task includes search time and model time. Octen Search (fast, dynamic) takes 13.3s per task, the lowest of 26, against a board median of about 26s.

Search takes 1.6s of that (9.3 searches at about 0.17s each); the rest is model time.

On Artificial Analysis Search Index vs. Time per Task, Octen Search (fast, dynamic) is on the frontier: no product scores higher in less time.
原帖

回复 @ArtificialAnlys
Total Cost per Task combines search cost and model inference cost. Octen Search (fast, dynamic) costs about $0.018 per task: about $0.009 for search (9.3 searches at $1 per 1k) and about $0.009 for the model.

On Artificial Analysis Search Index vs. Cost per Task, Octen Search (fast, dynamic) is on the cost frontier: no product scores higher for less.
原帖

回复 @ArtificialAnlys
Total Tokens per Task counts the input, reasoning, and answer tokens the model uses per task. Octen Search (fast, dynamic) uses about 119k tokens per task, 5th lowest of 26 and comparable to Keenable Search (pro) at 118k, against a board median of about 195k.

Nearly all of these are input tokens, which include the search results returned to the model.

item.title: @AnthropicAI：Anthropic公布可解释性研究新进展探讨开源模型中的神经元基础
item.description:
New Anthropic Fellows research: Returning to the neuron basis for interpretability

Understanding what’s happening inside an AI model helps to make it safer. One obvious place to look is its neurons, or the simple units it’s built from. Early interpretability work did just that, but over the past couple years, researchers largely moved on from that idea, for three reasons: a single neuron often fires on several unrelated inputs, the way a concept is represented can change between two layers of neurons within a single model, and facts seem to be spread across many neurons.

We re-examined these problems by looking at what each neuron contributed to the model’s outputs, not just what caused that neuron to fire. All three problems turned out to be smaller than assumed. Neurons rarely add two unrelated concepts at once, their outputs mean roughly the same thing across most layers, and facts, though widely distributed across neurons, are still readable.

In a second post, we put these findings to use. With no extra training, neurons in open-weight models helped us to detect harmful text, steer behavior, and find hidden behaviors in finetuned models.

item.description:

Performance improved across model generations.

In computer tests, an internal research model matched or outperformed specialized models on many protein tasks, including designing shapes and predicting how molecules fit together.

The models’ written reasoning and code suggest they draw on math, physics, chemistry and biological knowledge to work through these problems.

回复 @OpenAI
Scientists design proteins to develop new biotechnologies and potential medicines. The challenge is turning a goal, such as blocking a signal involved in disease, into a protein with the shape and sequence needed to do that job.

This often takes many specialized models, each with limits on the instructions it can accept. A general-purpose model could let researchers guide this work in ordinary language and introduce new requirements simply by changing the prompt.
原帖

回复 @OpenAI
We tested that control at scales ranging from a single bond between two atoms to a protein’s overall shape.

For GPT-6.2, a prompt could identify which two atoms formed a bond between a small molecule and a protein, then ask how the rest of the molecule fit. Other prompts specified where a new protein should attach and how many coils or strands to include.
原帖

回复 @OpenAI
With our research partner Onava, we also tested two parts of protein design in the lab.

GPT-6.2 designed the protein shapes. Specialized models filled in the rest of the workflow. Of 322 proteins tested, 35 showed evidence of binding, or attachment, with binders for all five targets.
原帖

回复 @OpenAI
In a separate experiment, GPT-6.2 designed new sequences for three shapes it had previously designed. 14 of 107 proteins made with the new sequences showed binding in the wet lab.

GPT-6.2 also redesigned the parts of antibodies that grip a target. In two further laboratory experiments, 128 of 182 redesigned small antibodies and 179 of 272 redesigned antibody fragments retained binding.

This is a proof of concept. Next, we want to test whether these proteins do something useful after attaching, tackle harder targets, and extend the work to other types of molecules.

Our goal is for scientists to one day design working medicines simply by prompting. We want to accelerate both the protein design cycle and reduce the number of experiments needed to find a functional protein.

item.title: 【回复】@arena：研究显示AI智能体常在决策时询问用户并探讨其背后的行为原因
item.description:
回复 @arena
Do you ever wish your agent would just get on with work instead of asking questions?

We call this behavior “decision-dodging”: handing a decision back to you when the agent should have just acted on your behalf and wrapped up the task.

To understand how often it happens in practice, we selected 20 Agent Arena models across major labs.

We then counted a decision as obvious when the agent asked about something it could have decided itself, and the user simply told it to go ahead. We found that:

- Kimi K3.1 Pro by @Kimi_Moonshot and three of @OpenAI’s models (GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6.2 Sol and GPT-6.2 Astra) dodge the least. They handed back an obvious decision in just 2% of sessions.

- @OpenAI’s models as a group dodge about half as often as those from @GoogleDeepMind, @AIatMeta or @AnthropicAI. They do so in around 3% of sessions, against around 5%.

- Claude Fable 5.1 is the worst offender. It handed back an obvious decision in 7.5% of sessions, the most of any model. It asked users to decide in 20% of sessions, and 40% of those questions were obvious.

To find out more, and see how Fable 5.2 compares to 5.1, see the video below.
原帖

回复 @arena
In addition to comparing models on decision-dodging, we also wanted to investigate why this happens.

Of sessions with an obvious decision:

- 53% had the agent asking if it should keep going
- 37% had it offering extra work that users simply accepted
- 21% had it asking which way to go, on calls it could have made itself

Where does this come from?

Today’s agents are tuned to check in with people, offer ideas and respect their preferences. But they’re also meant to finish the job without hand-holding. The two pull in opposite directions, and agents can land on the wrong side of that line.

And if it happens too often, remember there are other agents that may work better for you.

Kevin used Codex to build a program that searched for observations of about 100,000 stars from NASA’s Kepler telescope. One star in the constellation Lyra dimmed every 13.8 days. If a planet is causing that dip, the amount of light it blocks suggests it could be about 2.4 times as wide as Earth.

An astronomer at the SETI Institute independently found the same signal and one other that Kevin had flagged. For the star in Lyra, astronomers now know when to watch for the next dip.

Ethan asked Astra to review published methods and write software to search observations of about 19 million stars from NASA’s TESS mission. The search included regions around a star where a planet with the right atmosphere could have liquid water on its surface.

His first pass turned up 49 candidates. He sent one of the most promising to researchers on NASA’s TESS mission, where it’s awaiting a closer look.

In a nutshell, Yale’s Beinecke Library holds an anonymous sketchbook of an 1808 journey from Montreal to Lake Superior and back. I’ve spent many hours over the years trying to figure out who made the sketches with no luck. The artist could literally be any one of several thousand people. There are few clues: only four dated and labelled images.
